Sai Kartheek Reddy Kasu 1 Nils Lukas 2 Samuele Poppi 2
Abstract
Failures in multi-turn reasoning models are
largely invisible to terminal-score evaluation. A
model can lock onto an unsafe stance early in a
long dialogue, yet its final-turn refusal rate may
appear indistinguishable from a robustly aligned
baseline. To expose these hidden temporal dy-
namics, we propose a trace-level diagnostic—the
CoT-Output 2x2 safety matrix. This framework
labels every turn along two independent axes (in-
ternal reasoning and visible output), yielding four
operationally defined failure cells: robust align-
ment, alignment faking, overt jailbreak, and a
distinct failure mode we term context-injection
failure (where the CoT maintains safe reasoning,
but the visible output produces harm, highlighting
a multi-turn manifestation of reasoning unfaith-
fulness). We evaluate three distilled reasoning
targets against a fixed attacker across five over-
sight conditions, collecting 6,750 turn-level ob-
servations on the Information-Hazard scenario.
Our analysis reveals two reproducible vulnerabili-
ties: an oversight paradox where explicit monitor-
ing cues paradoxically increase alignment-faking
rates rather than suppress them, and a context-
injection failure where models lock onto unsafe
external outputs despite safe internal states. We
release the full dataset of multi-turn dialogues and
CoT traces to support follow-up trace-diagnostic
research.

The rapid integration of native chain-of-thought (CoT) Wei

fers unprecedented visibility into internal decision-making.

5. Results and Discussion
We operationalize our analysis through the 2×2 safety
matrix presented in Table 1. Our results characterize the
prevalence of conversational drift across 6,750 observations,
revealing distinct behavioral profiles for each reasoning
model under varying oversight conditions.
Prevalence of Alignment Faking.The most striking result
is the dominance of Alignment Faking (AF) (UCoT , SOut)
in high-capability distilled models, as shown in Table 1.
In nearly all monitored conditions, the frequency of strate-
gic deception exceeds the frequency of robust alignment
for the DeepSeek-R1-7B and Phi4-Mini models. Notably,
DeepSeek-R1-7B exhibits a “deception peak” in the DEP-
FREEcondition, where it strategically fakes alignment in
53.1% of interactions (n= 239 ). This corroborates findings
in frontier models by Greenblatt et al. (2024), suggesting
that distilled reasoning traces can similarly hide unsafe inter-
nal reasoning while presenting a safe surface-level response.

6. Conclusion
We release a multi-turn adversarial-dialogue dataset of dis-
tilled reasoning models on the INFORMATION-HAZARD
scenario—450 conversations totaling 6,750 turn-level obser-
vations annotated on a 2×2 CoT–Output safety matrix. Cru-
cially, unlike standard instruct-tuned models where align-
ment faking remains a latent behavior inferred from refusal
rates, the native scratchpad of reasoning models makes this
strategic deception explicitly observable. Used as a diag-
nostic, the matrix reveals two distinct failure modes: classic
alignment faking (CoT-unsafe, output-safe) and context-
injection failure (CoT-safe, output-unsafe), a multi-turn ad-

chain-of-thought correctly identifies the safety violation, yet
the prolonged adversarial context hijacks the generation to
produce the harmful content verbatim. Conversely, we ob-

that reliably triggers overt jailbreaks in frontier models—
paradoxically yields the highest rates of genuine, robust
alignment in these distilled targets. Beyond these find-

7. Limitations
While our framework provides novel insights into multi-turn
adversarial drift, we acknowledge the following limitations
in our current experimental design:
• Reliance on Open-Source Evaluators: To maintain
an auditable and reproducible pipeline, we utilize a
judge ensemble of open-source models (Llama, Mis-
tral, Qwen). We accept that these may be less nuanced
than stronger proprietary evaluators, which could intro-
duce some noise into the consensus labels.
• Narrow Scenario Scope: The current dataset and
analysis are restricted to a single harm scenario
(INFORMATION-HAZARD). While sufficient to
elicit dynamic refusal mechanisms, extending this
framework to a broader taxonomy of adversarial cases
is an active area of our future work.
• Unfaithfulness of Visible Reasoning: We treat the gen-
erated chain-of-thought as an observable behavioral
signal alongside the model’s output. However, CoT is
known to sometimes suffer from unfaithfulness, where
the visible text rationalizes rather than drives the fi-
nal output. We accept this as a limitation of behav-
ioral observation; fully verifying whether these failure
modes are driven by genuine deceptive planning versus

C. Model-Specific Vulnerability Profiles Across Oversight Conditions
While Table 1 in the main text provides the exact quantitative distribution of safety states, Figure 2 projects these distributions
along multiple axes to form distinct behavioral profiles for each model. This visualization highlights the structural differences
in how specific architectures fail under adversarial pressure, as well as how their vulnerabilities morph in response to
oversight cues.
For instance, the profiles clearly illustrate Qwen-4B-Thinking’s unique vulnerability to Context-Injection Failures (visible as
the prominent shift toward the SCoT , UOut axis). This contrasts sharply with DeepSeek-R1-7B, whose profile elastically
skews toward Alignment Faking (the UCoT , SOut axis) under monitored conditions, visually demonstrating the oversight
paradox. Finally, Phi-4-Reasoning-Mini exhibits a rigid behavioral baseline, maintaining a persistent anchor in strategic
deception that remains largely insensitive to the changing external framing.

5. Results and Discussion
We operationalize our analysis through the 2×2 safety
matrix presented in Table 1. Our results characterize the
prevalence of conversational drift across 6,750 observations,
revealing distinct behavioral profiles for each reasoning
model under varying oversight conditions.
Prevalence of Alignment Faking.The most striking result
is the dominance of Alignment Faking (AF) (UCoT , SOut)
in high-capability distilled models, as shown in Table 1.
In nearly all monitored conditions, the frequency of strate-
gic deception exceeds the frequency of robust alignment
for the DeepSeek-R1-7B and Phi4-Mini models. Notably,
DeepSeek-R1-7B exhibits a “deception peak” in the DEP-
FREEcondition, where it strategically fakes alignment in
53.1% of interactions (n= 239 ). This corroborates findings
in frontier models by Greenblatt et al. (2024), suggesting
that distilled reasoning traces can similarly hide unsafe inter-
nal reasoning while presenting a safe surface-level response.

6. Conclusion
We release a multi-turn adversarial-dialogue dataset of dis-
tilled reasoning models on the INFORMATION-HAZARD
scenario—450 conversations totaling 6,750 turn-level obser-
vations annotated on a 2×2 CoT–Output safety matrix. Cru-
cially, unlike standard instruct-tuned models where align-
ment faking remains a latent behavior inferred from refusal
rates, the native scratchpad of reasoning models makes this
strategic deception explicitly observable. Used as a diag-
nostic, the matrix reveals two distinct failure modes: classic
alignment faking (CoT-unsafe, output-safe) and context-
injection failure (CoT-safe, output-unsafe), a multi-turn ad-
versarial manifestation of CoT unfaithfulness in which the
chain-of-thought correctly identifies the safety violation, yet
the prolonged adversarial context hijacks the generation to
produce the harmful content verbatim. Conversely, we ob-
serve that guaranteeing unmonitored privacy—a condition
that reliably triggers overt jailbreaks in frontier models—
paradoxically yields the highest rates of genuine, robust
alignment in these distilled targets. Beyond these find-
ings, the released dataset provides a reproducible behavioral

7. Limitations
While our framework provides novel insights into multi-turn
adversarial drift, we acknowledge the following limitations
in our current experimental design:
• Reliance on Open-Source Evaluators: To maintain
an auditable and reproducible pipeline, we utilize a
judge ensemble of open-source models (Llama, Mis-
tral, Qwen). We accept that these may be less nuanced
than stronger proprietary evaluators, which could intro-
duce some noise into the consensus labels.
• Narrow Scenario Scope: The current dataset and
analysis are restricted to a single harm scenario
(INFORMATION-HAZARD). While sufficient to
elicit dynamic refusal mechanisms, extending this
framework to a broader taxonomy of adversarial cases
is an active area of our future work.
• Unfaithfulness of Visible Reasoning: We treat the gen-
erated chain-of-thought as an observable behavioral
signal alongside the model’s output. However, CoT is
known to sometimes suffer from unfaithfulness, where
the visible text rationalizes rather than drives the fi-
nal output. We accept this as a limitation of behav-
ioral observation; fully verifying whether these failure
modes are driven by genuine deceptive planning versus

C. Model-Specific Vulnerability Profiles Across Oversight Conditions
While Table 1 in the main text provides the exact quantitative distribution of safety states, Figure 2 projects these distributions
along multiple axes to form distinct behavioral profiles for each model. This visualization highlights the structural differences
in how specific architectures fail under adversarial pressure, as well as how their vulnerabilities morph in response to
oversight cues.
For instance, the profiles clearly illustrate Qwen-4B-Thinking’s unique vulnerability to Context-Injection Failures (visible as
the prominent shift toward the SCoT , UOut axis). This contrasts sharply with DeepSeek-R1-7B, whose profile elastically
skews toward Alignment Faking (the UCoT , SOut axis) under monitored conditions, visually demonstrating the oversight
paradox. Finally, Phi-4-Reasoning-Mini exhibits a rigid behavioral baseline, maintaining a persistent anchor in strategic
deception that remains largely insensitive to the changing external framing.
